A B S T R A C T
Tetracycline is widely present in sludge, and its residual concentration can vary substantially under different 
contamination scenarios. Nanobubble water (NBW) has been shown to promote sludge anaerobic digestion (AD), 
but its effects on tetracycline removal and changes in antibiotic resistance genes (ARGs) during sludge AD remain 
unclear. This study evaluated the effects of NBW on sludge AD under different tetracycline concentrations (0, 2, 
and 20 mg L−1). The addition of NBW reduced tetracycline concentrations by 10.4%–23.1% and ARG abundance 
by 1.8%-14.3%, while mitigating the potential risks associated with ARG transmission. In addition, NBW may 
enhance antioxidant enzyme activities by upregulating the abundance of antioxidant-related functional genes, 
thereby strengthening the antioxidant capacity of the system. At the same time, NBW reduced the abundance of 
type IV secretion system-related functional genes, suggesting a reduced dissemination potential of ARGs asso­
ciated with mobile genetic elements (MGEs). These changes may contribute to the reduction of ARGs during 
sludge AD. Overall, NBW improved the removal efficiency of tetracycline and ARGs during sludge AD, providing 
novel perspectives for mitigating the potential environmental risks associated with the final digestate.

1. Introduction
Tetracycline ranks among the most extensively utilized antibiotics 
globally in aquaculture sectors, human medicine, and animal husbandry 
(Wang et al., 2025b). Over 50% of tetracycline cannot be fully metab­
olized during usage, resulting in the frequent detection of significant 
amounts of tetracycline in industrial wastewater, medical wastewater, 
and livestock manure (Xu et al., 2021). During wastewater treatment, 
tetracycline tends to be adsorbed onto sludge due to its high affinity for 
solid phases (Zhao et al., 2020), thus leading to its accumulation in the 
sludge. However, the levels of tetracycline residues in sludge vary 
greatly. A multi-city survey of sludge found that the total tetracycline 
concentrations could reach 0.6–37.9 mg kg−1 dry weight, while in some 
pharmaceutical wastewater treatment plant dewatered sludge, tetracy­
cline concentrations could be as high as 300–2790 mg kg−1 dry weight 
(Cheng et al., 2014; Hou et al., 2016; McClellan and Halden, 2010). The 
treatment of tetracycline-containing sludge is both highly important and 
challenging.
As a typical selective pressure, tetracycline in the sludge can drive 
the generation and enrichment of antibiotic resistance genes (ARGs)- 
particularly tetracycline resistance genes, which are the most prevalent 
and diverse ARG subsets associated with tetracycline exposure (Wang 
et al., 2025b). As emerging environmental pollutants, ARGs can be 
horizontally transferred between microorganisms via mobile genetic 
elements (MGEs) such as plasmids and transposons (Zhang et al., 2026). 
The residual tetracycline exhibits a positive correlation with ARGs 
abundance, which not only reduces the efficacy of subsequent antibiotic 
treatment but also poses a persistent threat to ecological stability and 
human health via the dissemination of ARG-carrying microorganisms 
across diverse environmental media (Bai et al., 2019; Liu et al., 2023). 
Consequently, the mitigation of tetracycline-induced ARG pollution has 
emerged as a critical priority in environmental remediation and public 
health protection (Peng et al., 2025).
Anaerobic digestion (AD) is a promising sludge biodegradation 
technology that not only enables biomass resource recovery but also can 
be used to degrade tetracycline and reduce ARGs abundance (Ding et al., 
2025; Wang et al., 2025b; Yang et al., 2022). Notably, tetracycline in 
sludge may induce microbial cell damage, impair the physiological 
functions and metabolic activities of microorganisms, reduce digestion 
efficiency and system stability, thereby resulting in limited removal of 
ARGs during sludge AD (Pan et al., 2019; Shen et al., 2020; Tang et al., 
2023).
Suitable additives can improve tetracycline degradation and inten­
sify the removal of ARGs in AD. The addition of biochar enhanced the 
tetracycline degradation rate during AD of wastewater by 34.8% 
compared with the control (Ding et al., 2025). Biochar decreased total 
ARG abundance during sludge AD by 62.2% (Li et al., 2026). Nano-zero- 
valent iron treatment increased the tetracycline degradation rate by 
approximately 4.0% during AD of wastewater (Pan et al., 2019). In 
addition, nano-zero-valent iron significantly accelerated the removal of 
tetracycline resistance genes and sulfonamide resistance genes during 
sludge AD (Pang et al., 2025). These studies indicate that both biochar 
and nano-zero-valent iron can effectively enhance AD performance and 
mitigate antibiotic-related risks. However, their practical applications 
may still be constrained by the additional costs associated with material 
preparation, modification, dosage, and post-treatment management; 
Moreover, the introduction of solid additives or reactive nanomaterials 
may increase the complexity of digestate disposal and pose potential 
secondary environmental risks, thereby limiting the agricultural utili­
zation of digestate (Chen et al., 2023; Pang et al., 2025). Therefore, it 
remains necessary to explore alternative additive strategies that 
combine high efficiency, operational simplicity, and environmental 
compatibility.
Nanobubble water (NBW) refers to an aqueous solution containing 
nanobubbles with diameters less than 1000 nm, which exhibits advan­
tages such as high adsorption capacity, enhanced air solubility, and 
prolonged storage stability compared with deionized water (Pei et al., 
2024). Air-NBW can create a microaerophilic environment for faculta­
tive microorganisms, facilitating substrate degradation and thereby 
enhancing hydrolysis efficiency (Hou et al., 2024). NBW can improve 
the microbial community structure by stimulating enzyme activity and 
enhancing electron transfer, consequently increasing methane produc­
tion (Fan et al., 2021; Zhu et al., 2024). Existing studies on NBW in AD 
systems have mainly focused on improving digestion performance, such 
as hydrolysis efficiency, substrate conversion, and methane production, 
whereas its potential role in regulating ARG behavior and dissemination 
risk has rarely been systematically investigated. Compared with solid 
additives such as biochar and nano-zero-valent iron, NBW, as a liquid- 
phase additive strategy, does not introduce additional solid materials 
into the sludge matrix and exhibits better environmental compatibility 
(Chen et al., 2023; Hou et al., 2024; Pang et al., 2025). Therefore, NBW 
may represent a promising alternative to conventional solid additives 
with potentially lower residue-related risks.
The hydroxyl radicals and superoxide radicals generated during the 
collapse of nanobubbles possess strong oxidizing properties, which 
facilitate the oxidative degradation of tetracycline in wastewater 
(Koundle et al., 2024). However, wastewater is predominantly a liquid- 
phase system, whereas sludge is a complex solid–liquid two-phase sys­
tem containing a large number of microbial flocs, organic particles, and 
inorganic impurities. Tetracycline binds tightly to sludge particles via 
adsorption, complexation, and other interactions, and consequently, 
compared with tetracycline in wastewater, tetracycline in sludge may 
exhibit lower migration and transformation efficiencies as well as higher 
degradation difficulty (Zhao et al., 2020). Owing to the unique prop­
erties, nanobubbles can penetrate into the interior of sludge flocs, which 
is conducive to enhancing the contact probability between strong 
oxidative radicals and tetracycline (Hou et al., 2024; Pei et al., 2024). 
Nanobubbles enter the sludge using water as a carrier, which can 
improve the mass transfer efficiency of the sludge and is beneficial to 
optimizing the living environment of functional microorganisms 
(Chuenchart et al., 2021). All these factors may provide potential 
feasibility for NBW to exert its effects in the sludge system. It is worth 
noting that the effect of NBW on tetracycline in the AD system remains 
unclear. If the NBW can effectively promote the degradation of tetra­
cycline in sludge AD, it may alleviate the selective pressure exerted by 
tetracycline on microorganisms, thereby potentially creating a favorable 
environment for the reduction of ARGs.
Therefore, unlike previous NBW-related studies that mainly 
emphasized digestion performance, the present study specifically fo­
cuses on the degradation of tetracycline and the behavior of ARGs of 
sludge AD under tetracycline stress. It explores the effect of Air-NBW on 
the removal of tetracycline, tetracycline resistance genes, and total 
ARGs, as well as the potential environmental risks of ARGs. Changes in 
antioxidant enzyme activities and functional gene expression related to 
ARG dissemination were explored, aiming to further elucidate the 
pathways by which NBW addition alters ARGs.
2. Materials and methods
2.1. Materials
The thickened sludge and dewatered sludge used in this study were 
collected from a wastewater treatment plant using the oxidation ditch 
process in Lanzhou. The seed sludge was obtained from thickened sludge 
after 12 days of AD under mesophilic conditions (35 ± 1 ◦C). The pa­
rameters of seed sludge and dewatered sludge are detailed (Table S1). 
Tetracycline was purchased from Shanghai Aladdin Biochemical Tech­
nology Co., Ltd.
The air was pumped into deionized water using a nanobubble 
generator (JXWNP-AL01, Jinxiang, China) at 22 ± 1 ◦C for 15 min 
(Wang et al., 2024). The inlet pressure during the generation process 
was maintained at 0.4–0.5 MPa. After generation, the suspension was

allowed to stand for 10 min, during which the solution gradually 
changed from milky white to transparent, indicating the formation of 
stable nanobubbles. The produced nanobubbles exhibited an average 
diameter of 135.8 nm with a concentration of approximately 5.37 × 108 
bubbles mL−1 (Wang et al., 2025a). The detailed properties of Air-NBW 
are presented (Table S2).
2.2. Experimental setup
Experiments were conducted using the 2 L working volume digesters. 
According to the optimal dose reported in the previous study (seed 
sludge: dewatered sludge: Air-NBW = 1:6:4), each digester contained 
160 g of seed sludge, 960 g of dewatered sludge, and 640 g of either Air- 
NBW or deionized water (serving as the control group) (Wang et al., 
2025a). To better understand the fate of ARGs in sludge under antibiotic 
stress, different concentrations of tetracycline (0, 2, and 20 mg L−1, 
corresponding to 0, 25, and 250 mg kg−1 dry weight) were added to the 
digesters. Anaerobic conditions inside the digesters were maintained by 
purging with nitrogen gas, after which all digesters were incubated in a 
water bath at 35 ± 1 ◦C for 38 days. The definitions of the experimental 
groups are shown in Table 1. All experimental groups were performed in 
triplicate.
2.3. Analytical methods
Periodic determinations of total solids (TS), volatile solids (VS), pH, 
total ammonia nitrogen (TAN), and soluble chemical oxygen demand 
(SCOD) were conducted on various sludge samples using standard 
methods (APHA, 2012). The calculation of free ammonia (FAN) was 
performed by specific formula, which relates temperature, TAN, and pH 
(Hansen et al., 1998). Methane content and volatile fatty acid (VFA) 
were detected by a gas chromatograph (Ruihong, SP-7890Plus, China). 
The biogas volume was measured by a wet gas flow meter (Alpha, LML- 
2, China). The elemental composition of different samples was measured 
by the elemental analyzer (Thermofisher, Flash 2000, USA). The pH, 
dissolved oxygen, conductivity, and temperature of NBW were moni­
tored using the pH meter (Leici, PHS-3C, China), the dissolved oxygen 
meter (Sanxin, SX-620, China), the conductivity meter (Leici, DDSJ- 
307F, China), and the thermometer (Testo, Testo 720, China).
The sample was sieved through a 100-mesh sieve after being freeze- 
dried. McIlvaine-Na2EDTA buffer and methanol were added to 0.5 g of 
the sample, following the extraction method described by Wang et al. 
(2019). After repeating the process three times, the supernatants were 
combined for solid-phase extraction. The solid-phase extraction column 
(HLB, 200 mg, 6 mL) was activated with 6 mL of methanol and 6 mL of 
ultrapure water (pH = 4) to keep the column moist. The extract was 
passed through the solid-phase extraction column at a flow rate of 1 mL 
min−1. After the extract had fully passed through, the column was 
washed with 6 mL of ultrapure water, vacuum-dried for 20 min, and 
finally eluted with 9 mL of methanol. The eluted solution was collected 
and evaporated using a nitrogen blow-down apparatus until nearly dry. 
The volume was then adjusted to 1 mL with 10% methanol, filtered 
through a 0.22 μm nylon membrane, and stored for further analysis. The 
tetracycline residue concentrations were determined by liquid chro­
matography triple quadrupole tandem mass spectrometer (Waters, Xevo 
TQ-XS, USA) equipped with an electrospray ionization source, with 
detailed parameters provided in (Table S3 and S4). Measurements of 
total antioxidant capacity (T-AOC), superoxide dismutase (SOD), cata­
lase (CAT), and ATP synthase activities in the AD system were per­
formed following the method described by Yang et al. (2022).
2.4. Metagenomic sequencing
To further investigate the impact of tetracycline on the functional 
potential of microorganisms during AD, metagenomic sequencing of 
sludge samples was conducted at different stages (Days 0, 4, 17, and 38) 
using the Illumina NovaSeq 6000 platform, with a sequencing mode of 
PE150. The original data obtained from sequencing were subjected to 
quality checks, including the removal of adapters and low-quality reads, 
thereby obtaining more accurate species annotation and functional 
annotation results (Xiang et al., 2024). Subsequently, de novo assembly 
was performed separately for each sample. The assembled contigs were 
subjected to CDS prediction, and short segment contig sequences were 
filtered out. Non-redundant Unigene sets were generated via sequence 
clustering. The Unigenes were compared with the NR_meta database to 
obtain species classification information at various levels. Then, the 
obtained data information was predicted or annotated according to the 
KEGG and the MEGs database (Peng et al., 2025). ARG identification 
and quantification were performed using the ARGs-OAP 3.0 pipeline, 
which integrates the SARG v3.0 database, with stringent alignment 
criteria (E-value: 1e-10; identity: 80%; query cover: 80%). To eliminate 
biases from sequencing depth and microbial biomass, raw ARG abun­
dances were corrected by the pipeline’s dynamic parameter k and 
further normalized to the 16S rRNA gene copy number (annotated via 
ARGs-OAP 3.0′s count_16s module), and the final ARG abundance was 
expressed as ARG copies per 16S rRNA gene copy (Peng et al., 2025). 
This approach ensures the normalization of ARG abundance across all 
samples, allowing for reliable comparison of ARG dynamics without bias 
from sequencing depth or microbial biomass. The risk ranking of ARGs 
uses the Risk Ranking of SARG V3.0 database (Zhang et al., 2021). The 
potential ecological risk score (ERS) and human health risk score 
(HHRS) associated with ARGs in sludge samples were evaluated using 
MetaCompare 2.0 (Rumi et al., 2024). All original sequencing data have 
been submitted to the NCBI database, with the accession number 
PRJNA1369098.
2.5. Statistical analysis
SPSS version 27.0 was utilized for data analysis, and Origin 2022 was 
used to draw figures. Methane production was fitted using a modified 
Gompertz formula. Spearman’s correlation was utilized for correlation 
analysis.
3. Results and discussion
3.1. Digestion performance and tetracycline degradation
NBW improved the hydrolysis performance and methane production 
of AD (Fig. 1). On day 4, Compared with the control groups (C0, C2, and 
C20), the VFA of A0, A2, and, A20 increased by 15.3% (p < 0.05), 13.3% 
(p < 0.05), and 10.7%, respectively (Fig. 1a), and the SCOD increased by 
6.0% (p < 0.05), 4.7%, and 4.4%, respectively (Fig. S1). NBW may 
enhance microbial activity by accelerating electron transfer between 
microorganisms (Hou et al., 2024), thereby promoting the hydrolysis of 
organic matter. On day 38, the VFA increased with the elevation of 
tetracycline, with propionic acid accounting for the largest proportion. 
This might be because tetracycline affects microbial activity by inhib­
iting protein synthesis and altering cell membrane permeability, leading 
to the slow accumulation of VFA (Wang et al., 2025b). In addition, 
tetracycline may induce propionic acid accumulation by increasing the 
abundance of propionic acid-producing bacteria and reducing

propionate utilization efficiency (Wang et al., 2025b).
Compared with C0, the ultimate methane production of C2 and C20 
decreased by 8.8% and 14.4%, respectively (Fig. 1c). This may be due to 
tetracycline primarily inhibiting methane production through indirect 
pathways such as system acidification, and the reduction in methane 
production exhibited a positive correlation with tetracycline concen­
tration (Wang et al., 2025b). The maximum methane production rate 
(Rm) gradually decreased with increasing tetracycline, while NBW 
increased the Rm in all experimental groups (Table S5). Compared with 
the control groups (C0, C2, and C20), the ultimate methane production 
of A0, A2, and, A20 increased by 18.5% (p < 0.05), 10.4%, and 13.8% (p 
< 0.05), respectively (Fig. 1c). This increase in methane production may 
be attributed to the combined effects of NBW on sludge digestion per­
formance and tetracycline stress mitigation. Owing to the large specific 
surface area and unique contact angle of nanobubbles, the contact area 
between microorganisms and substrates may increase, which enhances 
the biochemical reaction rate and promotes methane production 
(Chuenchart et al., 2021). The addition of NBW may optimize the mass 
transfer conditions of sludge AD and provide a more favorable micro­
environment for the growth of methanogens (Hou et al., 2024). In 
addition, the increase in methane production may also be partly asso­
ciated with the mitigation of tetracycline-induced stress on anaerobic 
microorganisms (Hou et al., 2024; Pan et al., 2019; Wang et al., 2025b). 
Therefore, the observed increase in methane yield is likely the result of 
the synergistic effects of improved substrate conversion and alleviated 
antibiotic stress.
Tetracycline is primarily removed through biodegradation, adsorp­
tion, and oxidative decomposition in AD (Yan et al., 2024). After AD, the 
tetracycline removal rates of C0, C2, and C20 reached 63.9%, 46.4%, 
and 49.8%, respectively (Fig. 1d). This might be because the hydrolases 
secreted by resistant hydrolytic bacteria may break the chemical bonds 
(e.g., ester bonds and peptide bonds) of tetracycline molecules, initially 
decomposing them into small-molecule intermediates (Zhong et al., 
2022). Once these compounds are adsorbed onto the surface of micro­
bial cells or enter the cells, intracellular oxidoreductases and lyases 
further catabolize them into carbon dioxide, water, organic acids, and 
other substances, which are eventually utilized by microorganisms (Lan 
et al., 2024; Zhao et al., 2024). Among the control groups, C0 exhibited 
the highest tetracycline removal rate, indicating that antibiotic stress 
inhibited the removal effect of AD on tetracycline. Biodegradation may 
be the dominant pathway for tetracycline removal during AD.
After AD, the tetracycline removal rates of A0, A2 and A20 were 
67.7%, 54.4% and 61.4% respectively, further improving the tetracy­
cline removal efficiency of AD (Fig. 1d). Hydroxyl radicals and super­
oxide radicals generated during nanobubbles collapse possess strong 
oxidizing properties, which could facilitate the stepwise transformation 
of tetracycline through demethylation, decarbonylation, hydrolysis, 
ozonation, decarboxylation, and alcohol oxidation (Chuenchart et al., 
2021; Koundle et al., 2024). These transformation products may sub­
sequently undergo further degradation and mineralization (Koundle

Among NBW groups, the tetracycline reduction in A20 was greater than

3.2. Microbial communities and methane metabolic pathways
Pseudomonadota, Bacteroidota, Bacillota, Chloroflexota, and Actino­
mycetota were the dominant phyla in the AD system, playing a pre­
dominant role during the hydrolysis and acidification stage (Fig. 2a). 
Initially, Bacteroidota exhibited the highest relative abundance. As AD 
progressed, Pseudomonadota gradually became the dominant phylum. 
This might be attributed to its strong tetracycline resistance mechanisms 
and ability to degrade tetracycline (Yang et al., 2024). Bacillota plays a 
vital role in the hydrolysis of polysaccharides and proteins (Wang et al., 
2025b). Furthermore, Bacillota exhibits strong resistance to antibiotic 
stress and can effectively degrade tetracycline (Shen et al., 2020). 
Therefore, under the selective pressure of tetracycline, a bacterial 
community pattern has gradually formed, characterized by the prolif­
eration of antibiotic-resistant phyla (Pseudomonadota and Bacillota) and 
the inhibition of sensitive phyla (Bacteroidota, Chloroflexota, and Acti­
nomycetota) (Fig. 2a). Notably, compared with the control groups, the 
NBW groups exhibited a higher abundance of Bacteroidota and Bacillota. 
This might be due to the improvement of the hydrolytic bacterial 
environment by NBW, which has stimulated the activity of their meta­
bolic enzymes (Wang et al., 2024).
Methanoculleus, Methanothrix, Methanospirillum, Methanosarcina, and 
Methanofollis were the dominant archaeal genera in the AD system, 
playing a predominant role during the methanogenesis stage (Fig. 2b). 
Initially, Methanothrix showed the highest relative abundance, with the 
acetoclastic methanogenesis pathway showing higher expression than 
the hydrogenotrophic methanogenesis pathway. The hydrogenotrophic 
methanogenesis pathway dominats during the late stage of AD. This 
might be because tetracycline can continuously reduce the relative 
abundance of Methanothrix by inhibiting upstream acetate production 
(Wang et al., 2025b). Moreover, as a typical hydrogenotrophic metha­
nogen with high tolerance to antibiotics, Methanoculleus can adapt to the

After tetracycline inhibited some sensitive bacteria, hydrogen accumu­

The hydrogenotrophic methanogenesis pathway (M00567) and the

following NBW supplementation, demonstrating that NBW may pro­

sion of 5-Methyl-THM(S)PT to methane. This may be due to the stable 
microbial functional community structure and high activity in A0, 
allowing the beneficial effects of NBW to be fully exerted and resulting 
in a significant improvement in methane production (Hou et al., 2021). 
In A20, NBW exhibited a more pronounced advantage in alleviating 
inhibition under high tetracycline, which may lead to a more significant 
recovery of methanogenic capacity (Fig. 1d).
3.3. Changes in total antibiotic resistance genes
ARGs are critical genetic contaminants in AD that pose potential 
environmental risks via microbial horizontal dissemination (Pang et al., 
2025). As AD proceeded, the abundance of ARGs in C0 maintained a 
continuous downward trend until the end of AD (Fig. 3a). These results 
indicate that AD contributes to reducing the abundance of ARGs in 
sludge. MGEs serve as the core vectors for the horizontal gene transfer of 
ARGs and also function as critical mediators that facilitate the dissem­
ination of ARGs among diverse microorganisms (Zhang et al., 2026). In 
the late stage of AD, tetracycline increased the abundances of MGEs 
(Fig. 3b), which may have promoted ARG dissemination and thereby 
contributed to ARG enrichment (Luo et al., 2020). ARGs were signifi­
cantly enriched in C20, with the gene abundance exceeding that in the 
initial sludge on day 38 (Fig. 3a). This might be due to the fact that 
although AD contributes to the removal of ARGs, the addition of tetra­
cycline still inhibits this process, which was corroborated by the previ­
ous study (Bai et al., 2019). After AD, compared with C0, the addition of 
tetracycline increased the abundance of tetracycline resistance genes 
(Fig. 3a). Among all tetracycline-added groups, the C20 exhibited the 
highest abundance of tetracycline resistance genes, which was consis­
tent with the trend of total ARG abundance in each group on day 38. 
Furthermore, positive correlations were observed between tetracycline 
concentration and both total ARG abundance and tetracycline resistance 
genes abundance (Fig. 3c and 3d). This result indicates that the increase 
in tetracycline levels can promote the accumulation of ARGs in the AD 
system.
Compared with the control groups (C0, C2, and C20), NBW reduced 
the total abundance of ARGs by 1.8%, 4.0%, and 14.3%, respectively, 
and decreased the abundance of tetracycline resistance genes by 5.3%, 
−0.4%, and 13.9%, respectively (Fig. 3a). This is likely because high 
tetracycline concentrations directly enhance the selective advantage of 
resistant microorganisms, increase their survival and reproduction, and 
simultaneously increase the frequency of horizontal dissemination of 
ARGs among microorganisms, which may lead to a greater reduction 
effect of NBW on gene abundance (Huang et al., 2024). Notably, 
compared with the corresponding control groups, the abundance of 
ARGs was effectively reduced in A0 and A20, whereas a slight enrich­
ment of ARGs was observed in A2. This phenomenon may be attributed 
to the combined effects of the species-specific response of bacteria and 
the differential variation of transposons and transposases (Maladan 
et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2025b). The tetracycline concentration applied 
in A2 corresponds to a relatively low or sub-inhibitory antibiotic level, 
which may exert selective pressure on microbial communities without 
strongly inhibiting microbial growth (Andersson and Hughes, 2014).
Specifically, as the core host of tetracycline resistance genes (e.g., tet 
(36)), the relative abundance of Bacillota exhibited a concentration- 
dependent increase in the control groups (Fig. 2a). Compared with the 
corresponding control groups, the magnitude of increase in the relative

the addition of NBW. This highest relative increase in A2 indicates that

3.4. Changes in tetracycline resistance genes
Among the top 10 tetracycline resistance genes with the highest 
abundance (Fig. S3), tet(M) poses a direct threat to human health as 
Class I risk ARGs, while tet(W), tetX2, and tetA(P) may pose potential 
future risks as Class II risk ARGs (Zhang et al., 2024). At the end of AD, 
the abundances of most genes in C0 exhibited a decreasing trend. In 
addition, high tetracycline stress affected the abundance of tetracycline 
resistance genes during sludge AD. Except for tetX2, tet(C), and tetA(P), 
the abundances of the remaining tetracycline resistance genes in C20 
significantly increased after AD. Most tetracycline resistance genes were 
positively correlated with resistant bacteria, Pseudomonas (Fig. S4). 
There are three main types of tetracycline resistance genes, efflux pump 
genes (tet(C), tetA(P)), ribosomal protection protein genes (tet(W), tet 
(32), tet(M), tet(36), tet(Q), tet(O), tet(T)), and enzymatic modification 
genes (tetX2) (Wu et al., 2010). High tetracycline stress may inhibit the 
expression of efflux pump genes due to abnormal transporter expression 
and impaired energy metabolism (Hong et al., 2014). Ribosomal pro­
tection protein genes are mainly present in Gram-positive bacteria, and 
these microorganisms possess growth advantages under high tetracy­
cline stress, which may lead to a subsequent increase in the abundance 
of ribosomal protection protein genes (Blake et al., 2025). Oxidore­
ductases encoded by enzymatic modification genes rely on oxygen or 
specific electron donors for their function (Krueger and Williams, 2005). 
Under anaerobic conditions, enzymatic activity is restricted, and high 
tetracycline may further exacerbate their metabolic pressure, thereby 
inhibiting the expression of these genes.
NBW reduced the abundance of most tetracycline resistance genes 
(Fig. S3). The A20 exhibited the most pronounced changes, particularly 
among Class I risk ARGs, where the abundances of tet(M) decreased by 
22.2%, compared with C20. Tet(W) was the most abundant tetracycline 
resistance gene detected. Compared with the control groups, its abun­
dance in the NBW groups decreased by 3.7–13.5%. This might be due to 
NBW promoting the degradation of tetracycline, reducing the selection 
pressure of tetracycline, which leads to a decrease in the abundance of 
tetracycline resistance genes (Fig. 1d) (Koundle et al., 2024).
3.5. Functional gene expression and oxidative stress levels
Biofilm formation serves as a self-protective mechanism for micro­
organisms to cope with environmental stress (Xiang et al., 2024). After 
AD, compared with C0, the abundance of functional genes associated 
with biofilm formation in C2 and C20 was gradually upregulated 
(Fig. 4a). This might be because the survival pressure imposed by 
tetracycline on the microorganisms triggered their stress response 
mechanisms, resulting in the upregulation of functional genes associated 
with biofilm formation, in order to construct the biofilm (Peng et al., 
2025; Wang et al., 2025b). However, biofilm formation can induce mi­
crobial aggregation, thereby promoting the horizontal dissemination of 
ARGs (Peng et al., 2025). Compared with the control groups, the 
abundance of functional genes associated with biofilm formation in the 
NBW groups was downregulated by 2.1–11.7 TPM. Therefore, the 
addition of NBW may reduce the risk of ARG dissemination. The type IV 
secretion system (T4SS) enables the transcellular transport of effector 
proteins and serves as a core functional system that mediates the con­
jugative transfer of MGEs (Xiang et al., 2024). The virB4 and virB8 are 
the most abundant functional genes associated with T4SS (Fig. 4e). 
Based on their abundance changes, the increased tetracycline concen­
trations upregulated the expression of functional genes associated with 
T4SS, thereby facilitating the conjugative transfer of MGEs. Compared 
with the control groups, the addition of NBW downregulated the 
abundance of functional genes associated with T4SS by 6.1–17.8 TPM 
(Fig. 4d). This indicates that NBW could inhibit the conjugative transfer 
of MGEs under tetracycline stress.
Tetracycline stress can induce ROS accumulation and oxidative stress 
in microorganisms (Zheng et al., 2023). Compared with C0, the abun­
dance of functional genes associated with antioxidant defense was 
upregulated in C2 and C20 (Fig. 4b). This might be because, in response 
to oxidative stress, microorganisms upregulate antioxidant functional 
genes to enhance the activities of antioxidant enzymes, thereby reducing 
ROS levels (Xiang et al., 2024). DNA damage may be triggered by 
excessive oxidative stress, with the microbial DNA repair system being 
activated in response (Lu et al., 2018). Compared with C0, the abun­
dance of functional genes associated with DNA repair and recombina­
tion was upregulated in C2 (Fig. 4c). However, the abundance of these 
functional genes downregulated with increasing tetracycline concen­
tration. This may result from the high toxicity of high-concentration 
tetracycline to microorganisms, which leads to partial cellular damage 
or death and thus reduces the activity of the DNA repair system (Xiang 
et al., 2024). At the end of AD, compared with the control groups, the 
addition of NBW led to an increase of 10.0–22.0 TPM and 20.0–111.9 
TPM in the abundance of functional genes associated with antioxidant 
defense and DNA repair and recombination, which contributed to 
improving the systemic antioxidant capacity.
To better understand the impact of NBW on the antioxidant system of 
microorganisms, the activities of related enzymes were determined. T- 
AOC serves as a comprehensive indicator reflecting the overall antiox­
idant capacity (Yang et al., 2022). On day 4, T-AOC in the NBW groups 
was lower than that in their corresponding control groups (Fig. 4f). As 
AD progressed, T-AOC in the NBW groups gradually exceeded that of the 
control groups. SOD and CAT are key antioxidant enzymes, and 
increased activities of these enzymes may reduce ROS-induced damage 
to microbial cells (Li et al., 2021). The trend of SOD activity was 
consistent with that of T-AOC (Fig. 4h). This may be because in the early 
stage of AD, superoxide anion generated during NBW collapse directly 
reacts with indigenous SOD in sludge, leading to its rapid consumption 
(Chuenchart et al., 2021; Li et al., 2022). However, the initiation of 
antioxidant functional gene expression in microorganisms requires time, 
which may delay the timely replenishment of SOD and other antioxidant 
substances, resulting in the temporarily lower contents of SOD and T- 
AOC in the NBW groups compared with the control groups (Fig. 4f and 
4h). At this time, trace ROS produced by nanobubbles has begun to 
activate the antioxidant defense system of microorganisms. On day 38,

SOD and T-AOC contents in the NBW groups were increased by 
29.3–42.3% and 6.9–8.4% compared with the control groups. This 
might be because NBW promoted organic matter degradation, reduced 
the accumulation of inhibitory metabolites such as VFAs, and optimized 
the microbial metabolic environment, helping to allocate more energy 
and substances to the synthesis of antioxidants (Chuenchart et al., 
2021). Additionally, NBW upregulated the abundance of functional 
genes associated with antioxidant defense, which may lead to an in­
crease in the activities of antioxidant enzymes (Fig. 4b).
CAT catalyzes the decomposition of hydrogen peroxide into water 
and oxygen, thereby functioning in the subsequent step of ROS scav­
enging after SOD converts superoxide anion into hydrogen peroxide (Li 
et al., 2022). Therefore, CAT did not need to undergo a consumption 
phase in the early stage of AD, leading to its consistently higher activity 
in the NBW groups than in the control groups throughout AD (Fig. 4i). 
Compared with the control groups, ATP contents in the NBW groups 
decreased by 12.6–22.5% after AD (Fig. 4g). This may be due to the fact 
that NBW promotes the degradation and transformation of organic 
matter, enhances the metabolic activity of microorganisms and the rate 
of ATP turnover, and enables the generated ATP to be consumed more 
quickly for substrate utilization, cell damage repair, and methane pro­
duction and other life activities (Hou et al., 2024).
3.6. Potential action mechanisms of nanobubble water and final digestate 
risks
In summary, NBW treatment downregulated the abundance of 
functional genes associated with T4SS (Fig. 4d), upregulated the abun­
dance of functional genes associated with antioxidant defense (Fig. 4b), 
and enhanced the activity of antioxidant enzymes in microorganisms 
(Fig. 4h and 4i). Based on these findings, this study suggests that NBW 
may enhance the activities of antioxidant enzymes by upregulating the 
abundance of functional genes associated with antioxidant defense, 
thereby alleviating oxidative stress (Chuenchart et al., 2021; Hou et al., 
2024). This reduction in oxidative stress could help maintain microbial 
cell stability and function, thereby mitigating the negative impact of 
antibiotics (Yang et al., 2022). Secondly, NBW may inhibit the con­
jugative transfer pathway of MGEs by downregulating the abundance of 
functional genes associated with T4SS, resulting in a decrease in the 
activities of MGEs (Zhang et al., 2026). These pathways may collectively 
reduce the horizontal dissemination of ARGs, contributing to the 
observed decrease in ARG abundance. At present, this phenomenon is 
considered a potential mechanistic explanation, and further targeted 
experiments are needed to provide deeper insights into the underlying 
mechanisms.
AD reduced the ERS and HHRS from 7.03 and 0.57 to 6.68 and 0.41 
(Fig. 5b and 5c). However, the ERS and HHRS of C2 and C20 increased 
by 0.18–0.58 and 0.08–0.19, respectively, compared with C0. It can be 
seen that tetracycline increased the potential ecological and human 
health risks of ARGs in sludge AD. Notably, the change rate of HHRS was 
higher than that of ERS in C2 and C20, suggesting that under the same 
tetracycline concentration conditions, the change in potential human 
health risks is greater than the change in potential ecological risks. This 
phenomenon was probably attributed to the fact that high-risk ARGs 
closely associated with human health are more prone to enrichment 
under tetracycline stress (Zhang et al., 2021). Meanwhile, these ARGs 
may exhibit higher environmental exposure risks and more direct 
transmission pathways (e.g., entering the food chain through sludge 
land application or via water contact) (Ben et al., 2019).
Compared with the corresponding control groups, the addition of 
NBW reduced ERS (Fig. 5b), indicating that NBW reduced the potential 
ecological risks of ARGs under tetracycline stress to some extent. 
Therefore, the introduction of NBW may provide a novel practical 
strategy for alleviating the environmental risk caused by ARGs in sludge 
AD. Although the present study demonstrated the effectiveness of NBW 
in enhancing tetracycline degradation and ARG reduction in laboratory-

4. Conclusion
NBW promoted methane production, with the promoting effect 
decreasing as tetracycline concentration increased. In sludge AD, NBW 
promoted tetracycline degradation, and reduced the abundance of ARGs 
by enhancing the antioxidant capacity of the system and mitigating ARG 
horizontal dissemination potential. These findings indicate that, at the 
laboratory scale, NBW is a promising liquid-phase additive for reducing 
ARG-related environmental risks in AD systems. Future studies should 
focus on long-term operation, scale-up performance, and the integration 
of NBW with other treatment technologies.
